text: Before departure the leader of the outing talked his group through the entire route in some detail. Fill your bottles at the spring behind the mountain hut, he said, because the next water anywhere along the way lies beyond the summit. The opening stretch follows a deeply rutted track where it is easy enough to injure yourself. One of the walkers questioned the point of carrying a compass on a path that was already waymarked. Mist obliterates the painted marks, he responded, and a marker post knocked over misleads quite as readily as it guides. He asked everyone to tighten their rucksack straps for the climb and slacken them again on the descent. The group moved off with dew still lying across the grass, having agreed the rocky headland at the far end as their meeting place.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)

text: Old trading routes were shaped far more by the lie of the land than by sheer distance. A pass that rose too steeply meant harnessing additional draught animals, and that expense alone was enough to divert the wagon trains along a neighbouring corridor, considerably longer but easier going. Entire settlements grew out of that detour. A staging post appeared wherever the animals needed resting; a blacksmith established himself alongside; eventually a market gathered in front of the smithy. Then engineers drove a tunnel beneath the ridge, and the movement reversed. The wagon trains recovered the direct line, the staging posts emptied, and the town that owed its prosperity to the obstacle declined alongside it. Travellers today cross such valleys without suspecting why they are so quiet.

units: a heavily used path grows wider and wider

text: A well used path grows wider with every passing year. Walkers step round the puddles, crush the plants along the edges, and before long the route has become a bare strip with water running freely down it. On soft ground the process speeds up: soil that is already soaked cannot take the traffic and turns to a quagmire underfoot. Those who look after wild places have two answers to this. The first is a timber boardwalk, which lifts the walking surface clear of the wet peat and holds everyone to a single fixed width. The second is a bed of crushed stone rolled flat over a sheet of filter fabric, so that rain drains straight through instead of carrying the surface away with it. Either way, plants creep back along the margins by the following season, and the path stops spreading.

he leaves by the path that runs along the fields above
text: I had preserved a picture of a soft, rounded coastline with a great sweep of pale sand beneath it. Returning to that coast after years away, I found something else altogether. The sea had eaten into the foot of the cliff, and the wooden steps that once descended to the beach hung in mid air with nothing whatever underneath. A fisherman from the village blamed two winters of storms for the entire transformation. Where I used to run about as a child, water was breaking against bare rock. Oddly, it surprised me rather more than it saddened me. Nobody had excavated anything, nobody had built anything, and yet the bay had been dismantled. I walked back by way of the upper path that borders the cultivated fields, thinking that the shore of my memory existed nowhere any longer.

text: Three things are worth sorting out before you take the ferry across to a neighbouring island. Luggage first: nothing whatever breaks the wind on the quayside, and a bag left half open will empty itself in seconds, so strap down the outer pockets and keep your papers in an inside pocket. Waiting second: the sailings follow the tide, the time posted the evening before is often altered, and anyone with sense turns up at the landing stage well ahead. Seasickness third: the swell builds as soon as the boat clears the sheltered bay, and you will fare better standing in the middle of the deck with your eyes on the shore than shut in a cabin. And at the other end, nothing is bound to be waiting for foot passengers, so expect to walk to the nearest village with your load on your back.

text: At first light the workmen finally cleared the last slide of mud from the road over the pass. The job had begun at the thaw, after a slab of the bank had given way above the hairpin bend. Around midday a digger ground its way up the slope to reinforce the embankment, while two teams pinned steel mesh across the fractured rock face. The wind carried the dust out over the open moor, where half wild horses watched the machine without troubling themselves to move. Late in the afternoon an engineer walked the length of the carriageway, testing the firmness of the fresh stone with his heel. The barrier rose before darkness fell. The first cars edged round the headland at walking pace, and their lights drew a trembling line along the ridge, like a vein of fire opened in the rock.

text: A coastal dune builds itself in stages that anyone can follow without instruments. Dry sand rolls in off the foreshore ahead of the sea wind until something stops it: a tuft of grass, a piece of driftwood, a stranded plank. Grains accumulate in the shelter behind, a small mound forms, and the mound itself slows the wind, so further sand settles. Creeping grasses drive their roots through the fresh layer and anchor it, which is why the hump gains height rather than blowing apart. Once the crest stands above the reach of the waves, a second dune begins seaward of the first, with a damp hollow between them. Fresh water rises close to the surface there, and the plants thriving in it grow nowhere else. Cut a single gap through the crest, by boot or by wheel, and the returning wind undoes the entire structure.

he proposes honest signposting that sends people towards quiet valleys next door
text: Should we keep drawing crowds to wild places that crowds wear out? Local councillors are uneasy with the question, since their income depends on the visitors, while the people who live there put up with the congestion and gain nothing from it. The pattern is familiar. A view that is passed around on screens can see its traffic double within a single season, though neither the car parks nor the paths were built for anything of the kind. Closing such places would be unfair, and it is not the answer; spreading the load is. A free booking system moves arrivals across the week. A shared bus takes the queues of cars off the narrow lanes. Honest signposting sends people towards quiet valleys next door that are every bit as fine. What must stop is the selling of silence as though the supply were endless.

text: The woman who keeps the lighthouse describes her post as an occupation of patience, unlike anything her predecessor knew. He lived out on the rock for weeks together, wound up the wick, greased the mechanism and recorded the visibility by hand in a paper log. She monitors an automatic lantern from an office ashore, where a bank of screens flags the slightest malfunction. None of this saddens her in the least. The sea, she reckons, demands precisely the attention it always demanded, and the most dependable equipment imaginable will choose to fail on the night the swell rises. As a child she accompanied her mother on the runs carrying supplies out to the islands. Her predecessor held every reef in his memory; she locates each of them by its coordinates, and never trusts those alone.

text: Honestly, this newly opened coastal route is worth the journey, faults and all. The line of the route first: it clings to the water almost the entire way, swinging up onto the cliff tops and dropping again into coves barely wide enough to sit in, and it spares you the long tarmac sections that ruin so many walks. The waymarking next: clear, evenly spaced, no forest of signposts, though you hesitate a moment on the approach to each village. The facilities last, and here I do grumble: nowhere whatever to sit down, a solitary tap roughly a third of the way along, and dry toilets promised by the leaflet that exist nowhere but in the leaflet. What carries it, though, is the atmosphere: surf beneath your boots, birds skimming the waves, nobody whatever ahead of you for an entire hour.
